segments.text: This video will cover the setup of a Lead Prosper ping post campaign.
We’ll start by looking at a completed campaign to demonstrate how it’s set up.
To set up a campaign successfully, you’ll need your buyer’s API specs.
Here we have an example of Lead Prosper ping post specs
Here you’ll see the Field Name, the Type and Format, whether or not it’s required
in both the ping and the post, and a description of the field.
The ping will only send out partial and case specific information about the lead, such
as zip code or city and never contain the lead’s personal information.
Once the buyer has accepted a ping, they will be sent the post containing the full lead
information.
The description gives us the information that must be sent for these fields.
For static values such as lp_campaign_id and lp_key, the description will contain values
that must be hardcoded into the payload.
The description for dynamic fields such as first_name and city will use payload fields
to extract the information from the lead and insert it into the payload.
Keep in mind that your fields do not need to match exactly, as they can be field mapped.
As we see here incident_date from our buyer’s API specs is mapped to accident_date and currently_represented
is mapped to have_attorney in the campaign set up.
You’ll begin your buyer setup by copying and pasting the Ping URL from your API specs
and selecting the correct Request Method and Payload Type.
If you go to the “PING” section on your API specs, you’ll see that the Method for
the HTTP is POST, along with the URL, the Header Type and an example of the payload.
It says here that the payload can be sent as either a form or JSON.
It’s important to note that if you change the payload type from JSON to form or vice
versa once you’ve made changes in the payload builder, the payload will revert back to its
default and you will lose any progress.
So keep in mind that you should set the payload type before making any changes to the payload.
The payload will contain the fields that are laid out in the buyer’s API specs.
Those in bold are the fields that are required.
The first 3 static values laid out API specs, lp_campaign_id, lp_supplier_id, and lp_key.
These 3 values are unique to every Lead Prosper campaign and will need to be hardcoded into
every payload.
You can copy and paste these from the API specs into your payload builder.
Since these are Lead Prosper API specs, be sure to add the field lp_action test, so when
you test your buyer the Lead Prosper system knows this is a test lead.
You will remove this later after receiving a successful test response and before taking
the campaign live.
You’ll then map the rest of the fields from the API specs to the payload, for example
the first name field will map to the first name payload.
Pay attention to which fields are required in the ping, as you only want to send partial
lead information here.
Once again, your campaign fields do not need to match the buyer’s fields exactly.
The field on the left hand side of the payload in blue will be sent to the buyer, so make
sure that matches the API specs, however the green campaign field on the left just needs
to make sense to you.
As you can see here jornaya_lead_id and trusted_form are not required but those can still be sent
if you have the information.
And finally the required field sub_id1 is mapped to lp_sub_id1
Next is headers.
Content-Type is the only header per the API spec.
Content-Type would be the key and application/json would be the value.

metadata.title: Apollo & ZoomInfo Are Missing These B2B Leads (Here’s How to Find Them)
metadata.author: Will Butler
metadata.shortDescription:
Most B2B companies rely on Apollo, ZoomInfo, or LinkedIn Sales Navigator to build lead lists. But many local businesses, physical operators, and niche companies never appear correctly in those databases.

In this video, I show you how to use Apify and its Google Maps scraper to find hidden B2B leads that traditional sales databases often miss.

Using commercial solar prospecting in Central California as an example, I walk through how to identify farms, vineyards, ranches, cold storage facilities, food processors, hotels, resorts, and other local businesses that may be difficult to find through Apollo or ZoomInfo.

You will learn how to:

• Scrape targeted businesses from Google Maps
• Search by industry, city, county, and service territory
• Find company websites, phone numbers, addresses, and locations
• Extract available business emails and contact details
• Use Apify business lead enrichment
• Prepare incomplete records for further enrichment in Clay
• Build niche B2B lead lists without expensive annual database subscriptions
• Find local operators your competitors may be overlooking

In the example, I use the compass/crawler-google-places Apify actor to search for farms, vineyards, ranches, food processors, cold storage companies, hotels, and resorts in Mariposa County, California.

The same lead sourcing workflow can be adapted for:

• Commercial solar companies
• Marketing agencies
• M&A and investment firms
• Local service providers
• Energy and infrastructure companies
• B2B consultants
• Outbound sales teams
• Niche software and technology companies

Apify can provide the initial company data, including business names, websites, phone numbers, addresses, Google Maps listings, and available emails. The results can then be cleaned, verified, and enriched using tools such as Clay before launching outreach.

This is not just about finding more email addresses. It is about building a target market around the exact industries, territories, and companies that fit your offer.

Book a strategic mandate discussion:
https://calendly.com/sirodealflow/strategic-mandate-discussion

Learn more about Siro:

metadata.author: Austin Parker
metadata.shortDescription:
Want us to build this for your business? If you're a home service business owner doing $1M a year or more, book a call: https://go.optdigital.io/youtube

One Google Business Profile only ranks within about 5 to 10 miles of its pin, and in a dense market that can shrink to two. Everywhere outside that, the customer searching for your service gets your competitor instead. This is the four step playbook for running multiple Google Business Profiles in 2026 without getting suspended.

You'll see how to get your main profile into the map pack first, because there's no point expanding off a listing that isn't ranking. Then how to read a geo grid scan to find the pockets worth breaking into, how far apart to keep your pins so they don't cannibalise each other, and how to check the review count on the third ranked profile to know what you're walking into. Then what Google actually counts as a real location, a staffed address with permanent signage and a lease, not a virtual office. And finally how to launch them one at a time and get each one its own reviews by splitting your past customer list by suburb. Plus what to do if Google pulls a profile, and why one suspension doesn't take the rest down with it.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro
0:44 Step 1: Get your main profile winning
3:51 Step 2: Find where your next profiles go
7:11 Step 3: Make every location real
10:36 Step 4: Launch one at a time

respond, the better your ad performs.

a like and subscribe to Local View for

metadata.shortDescription:
This video walks through a step-by-step Google Business Profile optimization checklist built specifically for contractors who are getting wrong-fit calls and unqualified leads. If your GBP is pulling in price shoppers, small patch jobs, or calls outside your service area, this is where to start.

Most contractors set up their Google Business Profile once and never revisit it. The result is a generic listing that matches you to the wrong searchers, wastes your call time, and costs you ad spend with no recourse. This checklist covers every field that controls who finds you and whether they're worth talking to.

- Fix your primary category to the most specific trade option available, then add three to five secondary categories for every discrete service you actually offer
- Tighten your service area to zip codes where you've actually closed profitable work, and clear your address field if you don't serve customers at a physical location
- Rewrite your business description to name your service territory, project types, and minimum scope so wrong-fit callers self-select out before they dial
- Seed your Q&A section with five to eight owner-authored answers to your most disqualifying questions so expectations are set before anyone picks up the phone
- Build a review request system that asks customers to mention job type, neighborhood, and project scope, targeting 15 to 20 new reviews per month at a steady cadence
- Add local business schema markup to your website to match your GBP name, address, phone, and service area exactly, giving Google consistent signals from two independent sources

Mastering Local SEO & Google Business Profile Dominance

In the current search landscape, a Google Business Profile (GBP) is no longer a static directory listing; it is the primary "digital storefront" for any local enterprise. By 2026, proximity and relevance signals processed by Google’s AI have become the ultimate gatekeepers of consumer traffic, yet many business owners remain frustrated by map rankings that favor inferior competitors. Visibility in the "Map Pack" is the highest-ROI activity in local marketing, meaning a neglected profile actively cedes market share to more agile players. This breakdown transforms your GBP from a basic verified listing into a high-ranking, lead-generating machine, moving past the "set it and forget it" mentality to focus on technical optimizations and competitive audits that command the algorithm's attention. Understanding the strategic "why" behind these tactics is the first step toward turning a profile into a consistent engine for new business.

Strategic Takeaways for Growth

High-intent local SEO is fundamentally different from traditional search. While standard SEO prioritizes global authority, local search is a battle of proximity, immediate trust, and specific category relevance. To win, a business must satisfy the algorithm’s need for precise data while providing users with visual proof of quality.

* Prioritize your primary category over a broad list of secondary options so that you can outrank competitors who dilute their authority with irrelevant selections.
* Utilize the opening date "backlog" trick during setup so that you can establish an immediate competitive moat of perceived longevity and authority.
* Leverage GMBB Everywhere for competitive intelligence so that you can identify the exact service and category gaps between you and the market leaders.
* Aggressively pursue review velocity and "Local Guide" interactions so that you can signal active, current market dominance.
* Humanize your brand with consistent visual content and team-focused imagery so that you can build immediate brand intimacy and trust.

These high-level strategies are best implemented by following the chronological workflow established in this episode.

Timestamped Chapters:

In the fast-paced world of digital marketing, scannability is a vital component of user retention. These timestamped chapters allow you to bypass the basics and dive directly into the technical solutions most relevant to your current growth stage.

* 0:00 - 3:00: The 2026 Mandate: Why your ranking journey must begin at business.google.com and the necessity of immediate verification.
* 3:01 - 6:30: The Opening Date "Backlog" and the Single-Category Paradox: Navigating category selection traps and how Prince Creek Dental outranks Aspen Dental by narrowing their focus.
* 6:31 - 10:00: Competitive Espionage: Deploying the GMBB Everywhere audit tool to unmask competitor strategies and service gaps.
* 10:01 - 15:00: Beyond the 5-Star Average: Why review velocity and the "Local Guide" status are the only reputation metrics that matter for current rankings.
* 15:01 - 20:00: Establishing the Human Moat: Building post consistency and using team photos to build brand intimacy.
* 20:01 - End: The Citation Moat: Scaling with Bright Local: How to use professional tools to manage multiple locations and secure NAP consistency.

🚀 Find Commercial Insurance Clients with These 10 Lead Generation Tactics

Are you looking for practical, proven ways to find commercial insurance clients and consistently fill your funnel? In this video, we break down 10 commercial insurance lead generation tactics that independent insurance agents can start using right away.

If you want more opportunities beyond just waiting for the phone to ring, this one’s for you 👇

💼 In this video, you’ll learn how to:
📞 Leverage Call-In Business
Great when it happens—but why it shouldn’t be your only lead source

📣 Participate in Agency Marketing
Use blogs, videos, and content to position yourself as more than “just an agent”

🤝 Ask for Referrals Consistently
A simple habit that drives high-quality opportunities

❤️ Use the 30-Day “I Love You” Call
Follow up after a sale and uncover warm introductions

📄 Work Your Certificate List
Turn certificate requests into hidden prospecting lists

☎️ Make Outbound Phone Calls
Think of calls like lottery tickets—mindset matters

🚶 Do Prospecting Drops
Prefer face-to-face? Drop by and introduce yourself

🌐 Network with Purpose
Chambers, BNI, and community groups build long-term opportunity

🎯 Go Deep with Niche Marketing
Focus on one industry and plug into their associations

🧩 Build Centers of Influence
Attorneys, lenders, and accountants can send steady referrals

segments.text: The most common thing I hear about cold
email over and over is that it's illegal
or at least a legal gray area. And most
of the people saying it have never
actually read the law they're citing.
They've just absorbed the anxiety
secondhand.
In the United States, cold email to a
business address without prior consent
is legal and always has been.
The law was built around opt-out, not
opt-in. Almost nobody selling compliance
services mentions that part because a
one-line answer doesn't sell a retainer.
Here's the actual requirement straight
from the source and it's shorter than
most compliance guides make it sound.
The FTC's CAN-SPAM Act gives senders 10
business days to honor an opt-out
request once it's received. That's the
hard number the entire US framework
rests on for consent, not zero days
before sending, 10 days after someone
asked to stop, and the opt-out mechanism
itself has to work without charging a
fee or demanding extra personal
information.
CAN-SPAM was written for a world of cold
commercial email by design. It assumes
senders will reach people who never
asked to hear from them and regulates
the exit, not the entry, which is the
exact opposite of how most people
casually describe it online.
Cross the Atlantic and the model flips
entirely, which is exactly where most
confusion starts, especially for anyone
running one list across both regions
without separating them. CAN-SPAM
opt-out is the mechanism, no prior
relationship required, a valid physical
postal address must appear in every
message, and you have 10 business days
to process a stop request.
GDPR, legitimate interest is the
mechanism instead and it isn't
automatic. You have to be able to show
the outreach purpose, why that specific
contact's role makes them relevant, and
that your interest doesn't override
their rights as an individual.
Two entirely different starting points,
and treating one list under the wrong
rule set is the actual compliance risk
in practice, not cold email itself as a
channel or a tactic. GDPR's own recitals
spell out the mechanism senders in the
EU and UK are actually relying on the
legitimate interests of a controller may
provide a legal basis for processing.
Provided that the interests or the
fundamental rights and freedoms of the
data subject are not overriding.
That's not a loophole, it's a documented
defensible basis. But it only holds if
you can actually show the balancing test
behind it, not just assert it after the
fact when someone complains. And it
never overrides an individual's direct
objection.
The moment someone invokes their right
to object, the legitimate interest basis
stops applying to them specifically
immediately.
Back on the US side, the other
requirement people skip entirely is the
physical address, probably because it
feels like an afterthought compared to
opt-in versus opt-out. Every commercial
email needs the sender's valid physical
postal address, a street address, a
registered PO box, or a commercial mail
receiving agency address all satisfy it,
but the address can't be missing
entirely and this practice treats a bare
PO box as the weaker option even where
it's technically allowed.
It's one line in a footer and I've seen
recipients flag entire domains not
because the pitch was bad, but because
there was no address anywhere and the
message read as a phantom sender hiding
behind the domain.
So, here's what actually sits in every
sequence I run regardless of which side
of the Atlantic the list lives on. A
real physical address in the footer,
every message no exceptions carved out
for it's just a first touch. A working
opt-out mechanism honored immediately,
same day where possible, rather than at
the 10-day legal ceiling because faster
removal means fewer complaints
regardless of what the law technically
permits you to take. For EU and UK
contacts specifically, a documented
reason the rule is relevant before the
list ever gets built. Not invented
afterward if someone actually asks. An
accurate sender identification
everywhere, no disguised subject lines,
no spoofed reply-to address, no
misleading from name, because that's the
one thing both frameworks agree on
completely, without exception on either
side of the Atlantic.
Compliance isn't the obstacle to cold
emailing. It's the difference between a
sustainable domain and one that gets
reported into the ground within a few
bad campaigns.
The contacts I run against come from
Quora video, filtered and verified in a
way that respects the legitimate
interest basis before a sequence ever
launches. Instantly handles the sends
and keeps opt-outs suppressed the moment
they're requested across every sequence
and every domain in rotation.
InfraMail keeps sender identification
accurate at the infrastructure level,
and Aimfox runs the LinkedIn side under
its own separate consent rules entirely.
Know which law actually governs your
list, and the rest of this whole topic
stops being scary.

Chapters:
0:00 Can you go to jail for cold emails
0:25 What the CAN-SPAM Act actually covers
1:05 Why penalties are counted per email
1:45 Are you liable if an agency sends
2:11 Can a secondary domain hide you

3:06 The five rules for compliant cold email
3:59 Physical address and opt out rules
5:19 Honoring opt outs and your block list
6:37 Compliance is the floor, not the inbox

Description:
CAN-SPAM Act rules for cold email, in plain English. Cold email isn't illegal. Sending it wrong in the US is a federal offense.

Short answer: cold email is legal in the United States. The CAN-SPAM Act doesn't ask for opt in consent. It asks for honesty and an exit. Say who you are. Don't mislead in the subject line. Put a real physical address in every email. Give a working opt out, and honor it the second someone uses it.

Most people sending cold outreach have never read the law they send under. Here's the plain English version. What it covers, who's on the hook, and the five rules that keep you clean.

CAN-SPAM is US law and the FTC runs it. It covers commercial messages, so any email whose primary purpose is advertising or promoting a product or service. That's every cold sales email you send. It isn't the law that gets you every time. Here's the catch. Penalties are counted per individual email, not per campaign, so a sloppy send to a big list stops being a small problem fast.

Two liability questions come up a lot. If an agency or your SDRs send for you, you're still responsible. Outsourcing the sending doesn't outsource the liability. A secondary domain doesn't hide you either. Forwarding points it straight back at your primary domain. Anyone you email can report you, and the FTC or a state attorney general can act on it.

Then the five rules, applied to a real sending setup. Be clear about what you're selling. Don't mislead in the subject line or the body. Put a legitimate physical postal address in every email. A mailbox works if you don't want to publish your home or your office. Tell recipients how to opt out. Then actually honor it. Add them to a global block list. Don't just delete the lead list and keep emailing the same people. Easy to follow, easier to mess up. US law only, and this is informational, not legal advice.

The law keeps you out of trouble. It doesn't get you into the inbox. Domains, DNS and warmup do that. Across 300,000+ domains monitored, the thing we see most is a compliant sender still landing in spam. That's a deliverability problem, not a legal one.

What you'll learn:
- Whether cold email is legal in the US, and where the jail question even comes from
- The five rules every commercial cold email has to hit
- Why you're still liable when an agency or an SDR sends for you
- Why a secondary domain doesn't hide who sent the email
- Where compliance stops and deliverability starts

FAQ:

Q: Is cold email legal in the United States?
A: Yes. The law regulates how you send commercial email. It doesn't ask for prior opt in consent the way GDPR does.

Q: Can you go to jail for sending cold emails?
A: Not for normal outreach. The criminal provisions go after aggravated conduct like falsifying header information. Sloppy sending is a fines and reputation problem.

Q: Am I liable if an agency sends cold email for me?
A: Yes. You're responsible for the activity even when the sending is outsourced.

Q: Does this cover GDPR?
A: No. This is US law. GDPR and CASL are separate, and stricter.

Updated July 2026.

But sending spam, unrelated marketing, or selling the recipient's data doesn't fit. So, it's not enough to say this is business email, therefore it's okay. You need a real reason tied to that specific recipient or audience. >> Right? The point is that the purpose has to be specific and lawful and it has to stay relevant to the recipient's business. The article even says the moment the legitimate and relevant parts stop being true, the basis stops applying. That's why documenting the purpose matters. Not just thinking we assume this is fine, but writing down the product category, the target persona, and why that persona would care. That turns the outreach into something you can actually justify if anyone asks. >> And if the message is just generic blast marketing or anything unrelated to the person's business, that falls outside it entirely. >> Yes, the source is very direct on that. Generic mass marketing or irrelevant spam doesn't qualify. It also says harassment after someone has opted out is illegitimate. So the first step in the test is basically a gatekeeper. If you can't state a specific lawful purpose that matches the recipient's business context, you don't have a valid legitimate interest to begin with. >> So it's not enough to say email is easiest or we want to reach them. You have to show why email is the right channel here compared with other options. >> Exactly. The source says necessity is a comparative test, not an absolute one. Regulators aren't asking whether you could have avoided contacting the person altogether. They're asking whether among the realistic ways to reach that specific business contact, email is a reasonable and proportionate choice. If a less intrusive route could get you the same result, like a public LinkedIn post, email may not be justified. And for B2B sales, the article says email usually passes that test because it's the standard channel, less intrusive than phone calls, and it lets the person reply when it suits them. >> That's right. It's saying a well-targeted business email to a work address is generally seen as one of the less intrusive channels. The contrast matters. Unsolicited phone calls interrupt in real time, and SMS lands on a personal device many people treat as more private than email. So the article's logic is that email often survives scrutiny that cold calling and cold SMS often don't because it fits business communication norms and gives the recipient control over when to respond. >> So on balancing it's not just do I have a business reason it's also would this person expect it how much does it hit them and what protections are in place >> exactly the article breaks it into three checks. First, expectations. A CEO of a tech company would reasonably expect B2B sales emails, but a private individual wouldn't. Second, impact. One relevant email is low impact, while a barrage of irrelevant emails is high impact. Third, safeguards, easy opt out, clear identification, and relevant content all help. If the recipients rights and freedoms outweigh your interest, you can't rely on legitimate interest. So the balance can still favor the sender, but only if the message is relevant and easy to get out of. Is that the gist? >> Yes, that's the gist. The article says that for most B2B sales, the balance does favor the sender, but only when the email fits the recipient's role and the safeguards are there. It also says larger or more riskconscious teams often write this down in a short legitimate interest assessment. basically a one-page note explaining the purpose, why email is necessary, and how the recipient's rights were weighed. >> And that written assessment isn't some formal outside lawyer document. It just has to exist and be specific enough that you could show it if asked, >> right? It doesn't need to be drafted by outside council. It needs to be specific to the campaign and available if a regulator or a concerned prospect asks. The article also makes a bigger point here. The burden of proof sits with the data controller, not the recipient. So if a team skips the assessment, they might not be automatically non-compliant, but they'll have a much harder time proving they complied after the fact. >> So the practical move is to put that balancing test into a short lia for each bigger campaign and keep it on hand if anyone asks. >> Exactly. The article says larger or more riskconscious teams often turn the three-part test into a one-page legitimate interest assessment. It's basically a quick record of three things. What the purpose is, why email is necessary, and how you weighed the recipients rights and safeguards. The point isn't formalism, it's evidence. If someone questions the send later, you can show how you thought it through instead of trying to reconstruct it from memory. >> And it doesn't have to be some outside lawyer document, right? Just something specific and ready to show, >> right? It doesn't need to be drafted by outside counsel. It needs to exist, be specific to the campaign and be available to a regulator or a concerned prospect if asked. The article also makes a bigger point here. The burden of proof sits with the data controller, not the recipient. So, if a team skips the assessment, they might not be automatically non-compliant, but they'll have a much harder time proving they complied after the fact. >> Okay. And the article also draws a hard line between B2B and B2C with B2B usually okay on legitimate interest and B2C usually needing consent. >> Yes, for B2B cold email, the article says legitimate interest is usually sufficient and consent isn't required if that basis applies. For B2C cold email, consent is usually required under Pekka or e- privacy. So the legal starting point changes depending on who you're emailing and that changes how cautious you need to be before sending. >> So even inside B2B, not every contact gets the same treatment. What's the tricky edge here? >> The tricky edge is when the person is a sole trader or freelancer. The article says GDPR treats them more like a B2C contact even if they are doing business. So you can't just assume business email, therefore B2B. If the recipient is really an individual conducting business, you need extra caution and should be much more careful about whether legitimate interest really fits. >> So, it's less about the label and more about who the person is and how they are operating. >> Exactly. The article says the cleanest B2B case is something like emailing the VP of sales at a large software company using a corporate address that looks like an employee acting on behalf of an organization. By contrast, an individual freelance graphic designer at a personal Gmail address is closer to B2C territory, even if she's technically running a business. The more the person looks like an individual first, the more cautious you should be. >> And the article gives a rule of thumb for that line, right? >> Yes. The safer practical rule is, the more the recipient's role resembles an employee acting for an organization, corporate domain, job title, and an or relevant purpose, the more comfortably legitimate interest applies. the more they resemble someone who just happens to freelance or be a sole trader, personal email domain, no formal company structure, and a product that feels more consumer adjacent, the more you should treat it like a B2C send or at least do an extra cautious legitimate interest assessment. >> So, if I'm not sure, I shouldn't just lump them in with ordinary B2B prospects, >> right? The point is to avoid treating every business related contact as the same. Soul traders and freelancers sit nearer the B2C side. So the legal comfort you'd have with a larger company employee may not apply. That means the line is blurriier and the article's advice is to be cautious rather than automatic. >> So if a team's emailing people in different countries, the big move is to not just use one standard everywhere. >> Exactly. The article says sales teams selling internationally need to think beyond GDPR and can spam alone because the rules change by jurisdiction. It lays out different regimes for the EU and UK, the United States, Canada, India, Australia, and Brazil. The practical takeaway is to build your process around the strictest applicable regime for each recipient's jurisdiction instead of forcing one global rule that's too loose in some places and too strict in others. >> When you say strictest applicable regime, what does that look like in practice? >> The article gives Canada's castle as a good example. It says Castle is stricter than GDPR in some respects because its implied consent business exemption is narrow. It only covers an existing business relationship or a recent specific inquiry. That's a higher bar than GDPR's legitimate interest test for a genuinely first touch cold email. So if a list spans countries, you can't assume the GDPR standard will be enough everywhere. >> Got it? So the safest approach is to check where each recipient is, then follow the toughest rule that applies to that person. >> Yes, that's the idea. The article's framing is to treat jurisdiction as part of the workflow, not an afterthought. It also shows that the regimes don't line up neatly. Some require consent, some allow legitimate interest, and the opt- out timelines differ too. So the campaign has to be built with those local differences in mind from the start rather than sending first and sorting out compliance later. >> So it's not just have a lawful reason. It's a whole process. What are the concrete steps the article says a team should actually follow, >> right? It lays out seven. First, document the legitimate interest. Second, verify the email is business related, not a personal Gmail or Yahoo address. Third, make sure the message is relevant to the recipient's business. Fourth, identify yourself clearly, your name, company, physical address, and why you're contacting them. Fifth, include a one-click opt out. Sixth, keep a suppression list. Seventh, keep records so you can show compliance if a data protection authority asks. >> And the records piece sounds important. What exactly do they need to keep on file? The checklist says to keep the legitimate interest assessment, how the addresses were obtained, when and how opt- outs were honored, and the suppression list. The point is proof, not just good intentions. If you're ever investigated, you need to demonstrate that the process was followed, not just say it was. The article also notes that the opt out has to be honored immediately within 24 hours, and that the suppression list should make sure those people are never emailed again. So the danger is when the policy lives in one place and the actual sending happens somewhere else. >> Exactly. The article says teams often fail not because they reject the steps but because the steps sit in a policy document nobody uses dayto-day while list building and sending happen in separate tools with no guard rails. The compliant teams bake the checks into the workflow itself. list import checks against the suppression list, a campaign launch step that requires a documented purpose and an opt- out link that removes the contact from every future campaign automatically. >> So the bigger the sales or gets, the less this is about one rep making a mistake and the more it's about the system itself. >> Exactly. The article draws a line between no process, inconsistent process, and then full-on coordination problems. Early on, it says you don't need a compliance team as the first fix. You need basic structure, a real suppression list that gets checked before every send, a one paragraph documented purpose for each campaign, and a consistent unsubscribe mechanism. Once you get into midsize and enterprise teams, the issue is that those basics stop being optional nice to haves and become central controls. >> What changes at the midsize stage? >> Midsize teams about 10 to 100 reps move from having no process to having uneven process. Different reps may build lists from different sources. Some are more compliant than others, and there's no shared suppression list across the team. The article's warning is simple. If one prospect opts out from one rep, a different rep can still email them two weeks later, unless suppression is centralized. That's why a shared outreach platform with teamwide suppression handling starts to matter a great deal. >> An enterprise goes a step beyond that. Yes, with 100 plus reps and multiple business units, different teams can target the same accounts with different products while keeping separate lists and separate suppression logic. That creates a bigger risk that someone who opted out of one product team still gets email from another. At that point, GDPR compliance becomes as much a data governance problem as a sales process problem. And the article says that usually means a central data protection function, a companywide suppression list, and clear ownership of what opted out means across every team. So for a bigger company, the danger isn't just one rep going off script. It's that the whole setup makes it easy to miss an opt out. But what's the real downside if something slips through? Are we talking about those giant GDPR fines people always mention? Those fines are real, but the article says they are usually tied to much bigger problems than a few cold emails. The higher tier can go up to€ 20 million or 4% of global annual revenue and it applies to core principles like lawful basis. The examples it gives are major cases, Marriott, British Airways, Amazon, and it says those are extreme large-scale violations, not a single rep's outreach. So, the headline numbers are more like the ceiling for serious systemic failures. For a normal sales team, what's more likely to happen if someone complains? >> The article says the realistic risk is usually a formal complaint, a regulator's inquiry, reputational damage, and the cost of dealing with the investigation. It also says smaller B2B complaints can lead to a warning or an order to stop processing, especially if it looks like a firsttime good faith compliance gap rather than something deliberate or repeated. So enforcement can still happen, just not always at the top end fine level. >> Right? So the lesson is don't assume small means invisible. You still need the paperwork, the suppression list, and the central owner because those are what lower the risk if a regulator looks closely. Exactly. The article says the documentation from the sevenstep checklist matters because it reduces the operational cost and fallout if there's a complaint or inquiry. In other words, compliance isn't just about avoiding the biggest fine. It's about being able to show you had a lawful basis, a clear process, and immediate opt- out handling when it counts. >> So, even smaller teams can still get hit if they are sloppy. What are the mistakes people keep making? The article calls out a few common ones. One is treating B2B like a blanket exemption when it only lowers the bar. You still have to satisfy the legitimate interest test. Another is buying or scraping lists, then assuming the vendor handled everything. The article says that doesn't work because as the controller for your own outreach, you're still responsible for the lawfulness of processing. >> And what about the opt out side? That seems like the easiest thing to get wrong fast. >> Exactly. A slow or manual opt- out process is a problem, especially if it depends on someone replying and waiting days for a person to remove them. The article says that routinely fails the standard to honor opt outs immediately. It also warns about no audit trail for optouts. If someone gets readded months later, a timestamped record is what helps show it was an honest mistake, not a pattern. >> I'm also hearing that relevance matters more than just the company name on the list. Is that right? >> Yes. The article is careful about that. A legitimate interest to email a company's head of sales about a sales tool doesn't automatically justify emailing every employee there with the same pitch. It also says you can't reuse a list across unrelated campaigns without reassessing whether the original justification still applies because the assessment is tied to the specific purpose. >> So the practical takeaway is don't assume B2B makes you safe. Don't trust a shaky list source and don't let opt outs live in a spreadsheet. >> That's right. And the reason the article keeps coming back to documentation is that these failures create the exact problems regulators look for. Unclear lawfulness, slow suppression, and missing proof. Even when the issue starts as a firsttime good faith gap, the article says the realistic outcome can still be a complaint, an inquiry, reputational damage, and investigation costs. So, if I'm a listener trying to do this safely, the basic idea is cold email can be legal for B2B sales under GDPR, but only if you've got a proper reason to contact someone. You say who you are and you stop immediately when they opt out. And that's different from CAN SPAM, where unsolicited email is allowed as long as the opt out rules are followed. >> Exactly. Under GDPR, you usually rely on legitimate interest for B2B cold email because getting prior consent for that first business contact is often not realistic. But you can't just assume that applies. You need to pass the three-part test. Purpose, necessity, and balancing. The purpose has to be specific and lawful, not generic mass marketing or irrelevant spam. The email also has to be necessary and proportionate. And you have to weigh the recipients expectations, the impact on them, and the safeguards you use. And the audience matters too, right? B2B is usually treated differently from B2C. So, business contacts can often rely on legitimate interest while consumer contacts generally need consent. Soul traders and freelancers sit closer to the consumer side. So, you need extra caution there. And if you're working across countries, you should follow the strictest relevant rule because the position can change by jurisdiction. >> That's the practical side of it. A compliant process means documenting legitimate interest, checking the email is business related, making sure it's relevant, identifying yourself clearly, giving a one-click opt out, keeping a suppression list, and saving records. Bigger sales teams need stronger centralized controls because problems multiply when suppression handling and outreach aren't consistent. The risks are real. Penalties, complaints, and investigations, even if the biggest fines usually come from larger scale breaches. And the common mistakes are treating B2B as a free pass, using scraped lists, delaying optouts, reusing lists without rechecking purpose, and skipping the audit trail. >> So the short version is be clear, be relevant, be quick with opt outs, and keep proof of what you did. That's the difference between a workable B2B outreach process and one that invites trouble. Thanks for walking through it. That was Misar Reach on Misar Blog. Thanks for listening. >> [music]

**Penalties for GDPR non-compliance? **Up to €10 million (~$11M), or 2% of the worldwide annual revenue of the prior fiscal year, whichever is higher, shall be issued for infringements of: https://www.gdpreu.org/compliance/fines-and-penalties/ (https://www.gdpreu.org/compliance/fines-and-penalties/)
2. **What’s crucial about GDPR? **It applies to the data of the EU citizen, and how your company handles this data, regardless of cold emailing. e.g. Can I (as a citizen of the EU) have my data removed in your database at will? Private emails of people (in the EU) at the company you are targeting are off limits.
3. **Who does it impact? **Anyone/everyone with data on EU citizens whether or not they are sending cold emails.
4. **First, how you gather the data is crucial. What does this mean?**
    1. Companies need a pre-defined reason to collect that data,
    2. Ensure the data fits the purpose,
    3. You must prove who is involved in the processing of the data,
    4. And finally, ensure your subjects can have their data edited or removed from your system at will.
5. **What are specific restrictions for B2B cold emailing? Business emails only.**
    1. Opt-in vs Opt-out countries (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opt-outs_in_the_European_Union) - In the EU, currently states can choose to be in one of these two camps.
        1. Opt-out = you can target a B2B person - a corporate subscriber, and follow their opt out request.
    2. Compliance to the GDPR and the local laws/regulators.
6. **How does it change B2C cold emailing?**
    1. Not going to be possible in the entirety of the EU.
    2. It requires a double opt-in - form filled out, then accept the email they receive by clicking the link (confirming they own this email).
7. **Moving forward, best practices to maintain compliance if/when you are sending cold emails.**
    1. Do not buy pre-existing data - generate your data ad-hoc (create an audience definition). Verified and accurate (i.e. no longer with the company).
    2. Create valuable and highly-relevant messaging to each audience - make sure you did your research and you have something of value to this new audience.
    3. Be mindful not to be ‘spammy’ - generic high-volume emails to an unstructured and varied database (email list).
8. **How to learn more about this?**
    1. Join my newsletter (https://right2revenue.com/growth-tools-tactics-newsletter-optin/) (for anyone interested in growth marketing strategies…)
    2. Listen to my podcast on anchor or iTunes. (https://anchor.fm/marketing-automation)

metadata.title: Is B2B Cold Texting Legal? Every Law & Court Case Explained (1991–2026)
metadata.author: Kyle Banks
metadata.shortDescription:
Is B2B cold texting legal? I've been personally sued under the TCPA over cold texting — and I won. This is 35 years of law, every case cited, nothing hand-waved.

Ask ten people whether you can legally cold text a business and you'll hear everything from "absolutely not, you'll be sued into the ground" to "businesses can text whoever they want." Both are wrong, and both are wrong for the same reason: almost nobody has actually read the statute.

My name is Kyle Banks. I've been doing cold outreach since I was 16, I'm 27 now, and I run TaskBlink — where about 90% of clients use our data and systems for ice-cold B2B outreach over text. I've also spoken with attorneys involved in major federal TCPA cases.

This video goes back to 1991 and walks through every statute, FCC order and court decision that determines what a business can and cannot do with cold text messaging in 2026. Every claim is cited.

Learn how to scrape leads from LinkedIn post engagement and turn them into booked calls and paying clients with a fully automated LinkedIn outreach campaign. In this 2026 full tutorial, I show you the exact LinkedIn outbound system I use, step by step, inside Aimfox.

👉 Start your 14-day free trial of Aimfox: https://www.aimfox.com/

Most LinkedIn outreach fails because everyone is sending the same pitch to the same cold lists. The fix is targeting people with real buying intent: the ones actively liking, commenting on, and reposting content in your niche right now. In this video, I pull about 700 leads from a single LinkedIn post, build a lead list, and launch an automated connection request and DM campaign that runs on autopilot.

What you'll learn:
✅ How to connect your LinkedIn account to Aimfox and set safe weekly limits for connection requests and messages

✅ The intro message template I send right after someone accepts

How I'd Build A LinkedIn Outbound System In 2026

Most people overcomplicate LinkedIn outbound. In this video, I build a real campaign live - no slides, just LinkedIn and a blank doc - and walk through the exact system that actually books meetings: picking the right market, building an offer that works cold, list building, connection strategy, messaging, follow-up, and the numbers that tell you what to fix.

At Harriman Growth, the focus is on building intentional outbound systems that prioritize targeting, relevance, and quality over volume.

Known for a strategic approach to LinkedIn lead generation, Harriman Growth specializes in:

Identifying the right prospects for your offer
Building targeted LinkedIn lead lists
Writing outbound messaging that gets responses
Creating more intentional, scalable outbound systems

If you run outbound for your own business or for clients, this is the framework I'd use starting today.

Learn more at harrimangrowth.com
